Speed bin distributions for CE-CERT other buses by hour 5.1.3 Combined FleetDNA and CE-CERT Speed Distributions for Source Type and Vocation by Hour We now examine the speed bin distributions based on combining FleetDNA and CE-CERT data to increase driving diversity and confidence in results. Only source types and vocations present in both data sets that could combine are displayed to avoid duplicating result images; however, sources and vocations from both data sets, whether in common or not, are saved to the files SpeedDistributionResults_byHour_source_combined.csv and SpeedDistributionResults_byHour_vocation_combined.csv for sources and vocations, respectively. Figure 35 displays the speed bin distributions when the two data sets are aggregated into one, which generates robust data for all urban roads for combination-unit short-haul trucks. For urban freeways on weekdays, we observe peaks at 60 and 70 mph, with very little time spent under 50 mph, but more slow speeds during afternoon hours. We see similar trends for urban freeways on weekends, with a higher proportion spent at 70 mph during the early morning. Some lines on weekends may be more variable due to having less data compared to weekdays; we will see from the average speed section that hour IDs 1–5 and 17–24 have more uncertainty and fewer vehicle counts contributing. We recommend using the distribution from hour ID 6 for 1–5 and hour ID 16 for hour IDs 17–24 for urban freeways on weekends. With over 100 vehicles and often over 900 recorded hours per hour ID for urban other roads on weekdays, we can be fairly confident in the 5-mph main peak, which decreases steadily until 40 mph and goes on to a minor peak in distribution at 55–60 mph. The weekend trend is very similar, with some evening hours spending a higher proportion at 65 mph, possibly due to the lack of work week traffic. With edits made for urban freeways on weekends as described, all urban data for combination-unit short-haul vehicles could inform updates to MOVES3 speed distributions. 45 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications.
